bacteriophage: A split-panel illustration contrasting two eras of phage discovery: on the left, a scientist in muted sepia tones sifts through jars of murky sewage and soil samples under a magnifying lens, searching among scattered natural viral particles for one lucky match to a rod-shaped bacterium, with a small inset showing spiky-headed phages latching onto and bursting a bacterial cell while nearby human, animal, and plant cells remain untouched; on the right, in brighter, sharper tones, a researcher at a computer screen displays a rotating 3D genome blueprint of a phage being actively assembled strand by strand, with a robotic arm or synthesis device constructing a custom phage engineered to match the exact molecular profile of a specific antibiotic-resistant bacterial strain shown beside it, visually emphasizing the shift from hopeful natural discovery to deliberate, on-demand genetic design.
genome-language-model: Split the illustration into two mirrored halves joined by a shared spine of glowing, sequential symbols. On the left, show a classic text-based language model: a stream of words flowing into a neural-network diagram, with the network predicting and lighting up the next word in a sentence, evoking a chatbot interface. On the right, mirror the same neural-network diagram, but now it is fed by a flowing double helix of DNA/RNA bases (A, T, C, G, U), with the network predicting and highlighting the next base in the strand, which then extends outward into a newly generated genetic sequence. This generated strand on the right should visibly continue into a small lab beaker or petri dish labeled 'synthesize & test,' with a fork in the path showing most attempts fading into an X (failure) and only a few glowing sequences successfully forming a simple cell membrane or viral capsid (success), representing the gap between predicted and functional sequences. In the background, small labeled icons (a protein fold, an enzyme, an antibiotic molecule) sit alongside the genome model, visually grouping it as one tool among several in a broader 'programmable biology' toolkit.
synthetic-biology: A split-composition illustration divides the frame down the center: on the left, a strand of DNA unspools into glowing binary code and circuit-like traces, symbolizing genetic sequences being read and rewritten as data; on the right, that same code flows into a stylized cell or microorganism sprouting unnatural, engineered structures—geometric petals, crystalline lattices, tiny gears—representing life forms designed rather than evolved. Between the two halves stands a translucent human hand holding a stylus or cursor, poised at the boundary where digital instruction becomes living matter, gesturing toward a small lab-flask icon at the bottom that contains a miniature glowing cityscape of cells, hinting at biological systems engineered at scale for human use. Faint grid lines and molecular diagrams overlay the entire scene, reinforcing that this fusion of computation and biology is a deliberate, designed process rather than a natural one.
